clinicalPearls: Historically described as an osteochondrosis of a vertebral body producing marked flattening (vertebra plana)
Most cases originally labelled Calve disease are now recognised to be Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the vertebra
Presents in children with back pain and, sometimes, a mild kyphosis, usually without neurological deficit
Radiographs show a uniformly flattened vertebral body with preserved adjacent discs
The key task is to exclude serious causes of vertebra plana such as histiocytosis, infection and tumour
When due to histiocytosis it often reconstitutes with growth, and management is usually conservative
reference.pathophysiology: Calve disease refers to collapse of a vertebral body to a flattened (vertebra plana) configuration in a child. Although classically attributed to an avascular osteochondrosis, most cases represent an eosinophilic granuloma (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) that weakens and collapses the vertebral body while sparing the intervertebral discs. Other causes of vertebra plana, including infection and neoplasm, share the appearance, so the term describes a radiographic pattern with several possible underlying processes. When due to histiocytosis, remodelling and partial height restoration often occur with growth.
additionalDifferentials: Leukaemia or lymphoma involving the spine
additionalInvestigations: Spinal radiographs showing vertebra plana with preserved discs
MRI to characterise the lesion and adjacent structures
Biopsy where histiocytosis, infection or tumour must be confirmed
Inflammatory and infective screen as indicated
reference.prognosis: When due to Langerhans cell histiocytosis, single-level vertebra plana in a child often reconstitutes with growth and has a good prognosis, though outcome depends on the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign osteochondrosis without excluding histiocytosis, infection or tumour
Overlooking spinal instability or cord compromise
Attributing vertebra plana to trauma without a clear injury
management: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude infection or malignancy by biopsy before committing to conservative care
Manage a solitary histiocytosis-related vertebra plana conservatively with observation, activity modification and analgesia
Support the spine with an orthosis or brace during the phase of vertebral collapse and remodelling
Treat a symptomatic or unstable lesion with intralesional corticosteroid injection or low-dose radiotherapy
Assess for multifocal or multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis and refer for systemic chemotherapy such as vinblastine with a corticosteroid when disease is disseminated
Monitor neurological status and reserve surgical stabilisation for instability or cord compression
Coordinate care through paediatric orthopaedics and paediatric oncology, reassuring families that vertebral height often reconstitutes with growth
